reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID (Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease)
clinicalPearls: Caused by deficiency of sarcosine dehydrogenase (SARDH), a flavoprotein that demethylates sarcosine (N-methylglycine) to glycine in the choline-to-glycine pathway
Regarded as a benign biochemical trait, with sarcosinaemia and sarcosinuria found without a consistent associated clinical disease
The biochemical signature is raised sarcosine in plasma and urine
Secondary sarcosinuria can occur in glutaric aciduria type II (multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency) because the electron-transfer flavoprotein pathway is shared, so this should be excluded
Because sarcosine dehydrogenase depends on the flavin electron-transfer system, its activity may be affected in disorders of that system
No specific treatment is required for isolated sarcosinaemia
reference.pathophysiology: Sarcosine (N-methylglycine) is generated during choline degradation and from glycine methylation, and is normally converted back to glycine by the mitochondrial flavoprotein sarcosine dehydrogenase, which transfers electrons to the electron-transfer flavoprotein system. In sarcosinaemia, deficiency of this enzyme causes sarcosine to accumulate in blood and urine. Because the metabolite is not appreciably toxic, isolated sarcosinaemia is considered a benign trait. Notably, the same electron-transfer flavoprotein pathway is impaired in glutaric aciduria type II, which produces secondary sarcosinuria and must be distinguished.
additionalDifferentials: Glutaric aciduria type II (multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency) causing secondary sarcosinuria
Other benign aminoacidaemias on newborn screening
additionalInvestigations: Quantitative plasma amino acids and urine analysis demonstrating raised sarcosine
Urine organic acids to exclude glutaric aciduria type II
Plasma acylcarnitine profile to screen for multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency
Molecular analysis of the SARDH gene where confirmation is desired
Correlation with clinical status to exclude an alternative diagnosis
redFlags: Sarcosinuria accompanied by organic aciduria or hypoglycaemia suggesting glutaric aciduria type II
Metabolic decompensation, which is not a feature of benign sarcosinaemia and points elsewhere
Attributing unrelated symptoms to the benign biochemical finding
reference.prognosis: Isolated sarcosinaemia carries an excellent prognosis and is regarded as a benign metabolic variant requiring no treatment.
pitfalls: Overlooking glutaric aciduria type II as a cause of secondary sarcosinuria
Treating a benign trait as a disease
Missing riboflavin deficiency as a contributory factor
Attributing coincidental symptoms to the finding
references: Scriver's OMMBID: sarcosinaemia and disorders of glycine/choline metabolism
Nyhan, Atlas of Inherited Metabolic Diseases
management: Reassure that isolated sarcosinaemia is a benign biochemical trait requiring no specific treatment or dietary restriction

Exclude glutaric aciduria type II (multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency) with urine organic acids and a plasma acylcarnitine profile, since it causes secondary sarcosinuria and needs active management
Confirm the diagnosis biochemically with raised plasma and urine sarcosine, and by SARDH molecular analysis where clarification is desired
Correlate persistently with clinical status so any coexisting condition is not wrongly attributed to the sarcosinaemia
Offer genetic counselling regarding the autosomal recessive inheritance and reassure relatives about the benign outlook
